candidates.topic: The Capgras Delusion — Loved Ones Replaced by Imposters
candidates.teaser: Some people wake up one day and become completely convinced that their family members have been secretly replaced by identical strangers — and no amount of proof can change their mind.
candidates.video_title: Your Brain Can Decide Your Family Are Imposters
candidates.video_description: Capgras Delusion is a rare neurological condition where a person believes their loved ones have been replaced by identical impostors. It's not a choice or a lie — the brain physically disconnects facial recognition from emotional response.
candidates.script: A man woke up one morning, looked at his wife of 30 years, and calmly told doctors she was an imposter. Same face, same voice — but to him, a stranger. Capgras Delusion happens when the brain's facial recognition system disconnects from its emotional center. You see someone familiar but feel nothing, so your brain invents the only logical explanation: replacement. It's not psychosis. It's a wiring failure. The question is — how would you prove you're really you?

candidates.topic: The Dyeing Coral — Great Barrier Reef Bleaching Speed
candidates.teaser: The largest living structure on Earth is vanishing at a speed scientists didn't think possible just a decade ago — and the timeline left is shorter than most people's mortgages.
candidates.video_title: The World's Largest Living Thing Is Dying Fast
candidates.video_description: The Great Barrier Reef has lost over 50% of its coral cover since 1995. Mass bleaching events now occur so frequently the reef can no longer recover between them. What was once a 10,000-year-old ecosystem may functionally collapse within decades.
candidates.script: The Great Barrier Reef survived ice ages, meteor impacts, and five mass extinctions — then in 2022, it bleached for the fourth time in seven years. Coral bleaching happens when water gets too warm: the coral expels the algae keeping it alive and turns bone white. Below 30% cover, a reef cannot recover. The Great Barrier Reef is already at 50% loss since 1995. It is 2,300 kilometers long and visible from space. In fifty years, your grandchildren may only see it in photographs.

candidates.topic: The Hexagon Storm — Saturn's Geometric Hurricane
candidates.teaser: There is a perfectly geometric six-sided storm on Saturn that has been spinning continuously for at least 40 years — and nobody fully understands why nature drew a hexagon in space.
candidates.video_title: Saturn Has a Perfect Hexagon Bigger Than Earth
candidates.video_description: Saturn's north pole hosts a hurricane-shaped hexagonal storm roughly 30,000 kilometers wide — large enough to swallow four Earths. Discovered by Voyager in 1981, it has persisted for decades and changes color with Saturn's seasons, shifting from blue to gold.
candidates.script: There is a six-sided storm on Saturn so geometrically perfect it looks computer-generated. Each side is longer than Earth's diameter. It has been spinning nonstop since at least 1981, when Voyager first photographed it — and we still cannot fully explain why fluid dynamics produce a hexagon instead of a circle. It shifts color from blue to gold as Saturn's seasons change. Whatever is driving that shape has lasted longer than most human civilizations. Nature drew a hexagon 1.4 billion kilometers away. Why?

candidates.topic: The Library of Ashurbanipal — World's First Organized Archive
candidates.teaser: Over 2,600 years ago, one Assyrian king became so obsessed with collecting all human knowledge that he essentially invented the concept of a library — and the tablets he buried still hold stories we haven't finished translating.
candidates.video_title: He Collected Every Book on Earth — in 650 BC
candidates.video_description: King Ashurbanipal of Assyria assembled over 30,000 clay tablets in Nineveh around 650 BC, creating humanity's first systematically organized library. Among them was the Epic of Gilgamesh — the world's oldest written story. The library was buried for 2,500 years before archaeologists uncovered it in the 1850s.
candidates.script: In 650 BC, a king sent royal agents across the known world with one order: copy every text that exists and bring it to me. King Ashurbanipal of Assyria built a library of over 30,000 clay tablets — catalogued, shelved, and indexed. Inside was the Epic of Gilgamesh, humanity's oldest written story, buried for 2,500 years until British archaeologists dug it up in the 1850s. We'd never heard of a great flood story before that tablet. Imagine what's still untranslated.

candidates.topic: The Immortal Cell Line — Henrietta Lacks and HeLa Cells
candidates.teaser: A woman died from cancer in 1951 — but her cells never did, and without her knowledge or permission, they went on to fuel nearly every major medical breakthrough of the past 70 years.
candidates.video_title: She Died in 1951. Her Cells Are Still Alive Today.
candidates.video_description: Henrietta Lacks was a Black American woman whose cancer cells were harvested without consent in 1951. Those cells — dubbed HeLa — became the first immortal human cell line, contributing to the polio vaccine, cancer research, and COVID-19 treatments. Her family didn't learn of it until 1975.
candidates.script: Henrietta Lacks died of cervical cancer in 1951. But before she did, a doctor took a sample of her tumor without asking. Those cells did something no human cells had ever done — they refused to die. HeLa cells have been multiplying in laboratories for 73 years. They helped create the polio vaccine, early cancer treatments, and COVID-19 research. If you weighed every HeLa cell ever grown, it would exceed 50 million metric tons. Her family learned about it 24 years after her death. Was that science — or theft?
